360 Degrees: My First Post as Acting Municipal Treasurer

Two years, two Mayors, a pandemic, a typhoon and an election: what my first post as Acting Municipal Treasurer of Mulanay, Quezon, taught me.

Some assignments arrive with a job description. Mine arrived with a microphone, a restaurant full of masked faces, and a turnover that took two full days.

I received my first designation as Acting Municipal Treasurer of Mulanay, Quezon, at a time when I was the only ICLTE passer in the Provincial Treasurer's Office. An Acting Municipal Treasurer must have passed the Basic Competency on Local Treasury Examination (BCLTE); the Intermediate Competency on Local Treasury Examination (ICLTE) is the higher of the two. That credential opened a door I had not expected to walk through so soon. On the road to Mulanay, one quiet question kept me company: am I ready for this?

Mulanay sits on the Bondoc Peninsula in southern Quezon, a short trip from my hometown of San Andres. It is a town of 28 barangays and 55,576 people, according to the 2020 Census. The place was not new to me, but the office was. What followed, from 2020 to 2022, were two of the most demanding and meaningful years of my career, spent in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic. This is the story of that first post.

A Welcome I Did Not Expect

I arrived in Mulanay at around two in the afternoon, ready for paperwork. I was not ready for the warmth that waited for me that evening.

We gathered at a local restaurant for a dinner with two purposes: to thank the outgoing Municipal Treasurer for the service given to the town, and to welcome me as the new one. Around the tables sat the Municipal Mayor, the Vice Mayor, every member of the Sangguniang Bayan, the Municipal Administrator, the department heads and a few employees of the municipality.

Every face around the tables was half hidden behind a mask. It was the pandemic, and I learned to read smiles in people's eyes. Among them was a familiar one: the Municipal Assessor, my friend and former co-worker at the Provincial Treasurer's Office. In a room full of new colleagues, one friendly face made all the difference.

Then someone handed me the microphone. I thanked everyone for receiving me, and I told them the truth:

This is a challenge for me. My comfort zone has always been one division. Here, I will have to work and decide in 360 degrees.

The next two days belonged to the turnover, formally conducted by a team from the Provincial Treasurer's Office. In treasury work, a turnover is more than a handshake. It is the moment accountability changes hands, as cash, records and responsibility pass from one officer to the next.

From One Division to 360 Degrees

Until then, my work had clear borders. I belonged to a single division with a defined set of tasks, and I knew that ground well.

Mulanay erased those borders. As head of the treasury office, I suddenly owned the whole circle: collections, disbursements, cash management, reports, people, and the decisions that tie them together. Problems no longer came from one direction. They came from every side, often at once, and the final call was mine.

That shift is the real test of a first designation. It is not about knowing more rules. It is about seeing the whole office at once and still deciding with care.

Home Was a Container House

The pandemic shaped every part of those years. Travel was restricted, offices ran on skeleton schedules, and going home was rarely an option.

For two years, my home was the municipal container house in Mulanay. It was small and simple, but it kept me close to the office and the work. It stood near the sea, and every night I fell asleep to the sound of the waves. I wore a face mask every working day, until it felt as much a part of my uniform as my ID.

Those nights by the sea taught me something about public service: you cannot always choose your conditions, but you can choose how you show up in them. I am deeply grateful to the people of Mulanay who made those years easier. They checked on me, helped me settle in, and treated the new treasurer like one of their own.

Three Days in Boracay

In those years we could hardly go anywhere. Lockdowns and travel restrictions kept most of us within town limits for months at a time.

So when the first Mayor I served approved my travel to Boracay for a three-day official training, it felt like a rare gift. The training sharpened my skills as a new treasurer, and the short change of scenery sent me back to Mulanay with fresh energy. I remain thankful for that trust, at a time when every trip had to be justified.

When the Typhoon Came

As if a pandemic were not enough, a strong typhoon struck Mulanay during my term. Homes were damaged, livelihoods were lost, and families waited for help.

In a disaster, the treasury is where help becomes cash in people's hands. Together with the municipal officials, headed by the Municipal Mayor, my staff and I visited all 28 barangays to distribute financial assistance to the affected families. It took about a week, and I could not have done it without the responsible, hardworking team beside me.

I came to know the town not from behind a desk, but from its roads, its coastline and its upland villages. Those trips changed how I understand my job.

Every peso we safeguard in the government account exists for moments like that: a family receiving help when they need it most.

Election Duty: Neutral by Mandate

I also served through an election in Mulanay. I will leave the politics to others; that is not my place, and it never should be.

What I can say is this: the law gives the municipal treasurer a role in the election, including the counting and canvassing of votes. It is one of the least visible parts of the job, and one of the most serious. On those days, neutrality is not just good manners. It is the duty itself.

Two Mayors, One Team

During my term I served under two Mayors: the first for one year and ten months, and the second for my final two months. Leadership changed, but the work never paused.

What made that possible was the people. We worked well together across the whole municipality, from the department heads to the frontline staff. In the middle of a pandemic, that kind of teamwork is not a bonus. It is how a town keeps running.

What the Job Taught Me

The work of a municipal treasurer is not easy, and the accountability is high. Every collection, every disbursement and every signature carries your name, and you answer for all of it. Mulanay taught me three lessons I still carry:

Leadership begins outside your comfort zone. I grew the most when I had to see the whole office, not just one division.

Public money has a human face. A week on the road to all 28 barangays after the typhoon made that real for me.

No one serves alone. A pandemic, a typhoon and an election were easier to face because of the people beside me.

Thank You, Mulanay

Looking back, I am truly happy for the experience and the work. To the two Mayors I served, the Vice Mayor, the Sangguniang Bayan, the Municipal Administrator, the department heads, my treasury staff, my friend the Municipal Assessor, and the people of Mulanay: thank you for welcoming a neighbor from San Andres and making me one of your own.

And to anyone receiving a first designation today: say yes to the challenge. The comfort zone is safe, but the growth is out there, all 360 degrees of it.

Population and barangay figures: PhilAtlas, Mulanay, Province of Quezon, based on the 2020 Census.

The ALTOS Framework, Principle 1: Legality First

Before we ask how a peso was handled, we should ask whether the law allowed it at all.

Ask any treasury clerk what their job is, and most will say they receive payments and release checks. That is true, but it skips a step. Behind every peso that crosses the counter, in or out, there should be a rule that says it may. The ALTOS Framework has ten principles, and this first one is about that unseen step.

A word about the series before we begin. The framework is the closing part of my book, 360° Accountability. Each of its ten principles pairs an idea from one of the thinkers who shaped public administration with a Philippine law, and then with a habit a treasury office can start using tomorrow, with or without a computer. I will take them one at a time, in order, because each one rests on the one before it.

Why principles, and not just another manual? The Philippines already has good manuals. Manuals tell an officer what to do when the case is ordinary. Principles tell the officer what to do when the case is new. What is often missing is a shared understanding of why the manuals say what they say. Without it, procedures slowly turn into rituals, and rituals are the first thing dropped when the office gets busy. The emblem of ALTOS is a full 360° ring for the same reason: accountability that covers only 300 degrees leaves a gap, and money leaks through gaps.

No legal basis, no transaction. If a peso cannot point to the rule that allows it, it should not move.

Two Roles, One Line Between Them

Local government works because two groups do two different jobs. The Sanggunian, as the local lawmaking body, chooses what to tax, what to charge, and what to spend on. The treasury carries out those choices. In 1900 the American scholar Frank Goodnow described this as the difference between expressing the will of the public and executing it. Later writers argued that the two can never be fully separated, and they had a point, but as a division of labor the idea still holds. In a treasury office it is not theory: it is the daily difference between doing your job and overstepping it.

A treasurer can recommend a new rate, point out a fee that no longer makes sense, or warn that a budget line is running low. What a treasurer cannot do is make up a charge on the spot, or pay for something the council never funded, however reasonable it may seem at the time.

Woodrow Wilson, writing even earlier, in 1887, observed that running a constitution is harder than framing one, and argued that administration deserves to be studied as a business-like field of its own, apart from the making of policy. Our law reflects that view too. Under Section 470 of the Local Government Code, the treasurer is appointed by the Secretary of Finance from a list of at least three nominees of the mayor, and works under the mayor's administrative supervision. The arrangement keeps the collection of revenue professional and uniform from one town to the next, and it lets the treasurer serve each administration the same way. The tax ordinance is applied identically to every taxpayer, whoever is in office.

The Code also spells out the treasurer's duties: taking custody of and managing local funds; taking charge of their disbursement; collecting taxes, fees and charges, and inspecting businesses for compliance with tax ordinances; keeping tax information up to date; advising the mayor and the Sanggunian on fiscal matters, including the income estimates used for the budget; and certifying whether cash is available for an obligation. Every one of these duties carries out decisions that others wrote into law. None of them gives the power to make new ones.

Where the Authority Comes From

It helps to picture legal authority as a chain with several links. At the top is the 1987 Constitution. Article X, Section 5 lets each local government create its own sources of revenue and levy taxes, fees and charges, but only within guidelines that Congress sets. Article IX-D creates the Commission on Audit and gives it power over every government peso, earned or spent. So local fiscal autonomy is real, but it is autonomy under audit, never autonomy from it.

The next link is the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), which turns those constitutional grants into working rules. Then come the municipality's own ordinances: the revenue code that sets rates and fees, and the annual appropriation ordinance that sets what may be spent. For a municipality, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan reviews both the tax ordinances and the annual budget. The last link is the official receipt or the check itself. A transaction is legal only when every link above it holds.

What the Code Requires on the Collection Side

Section 130 of the Code lists the ground rules for local taxes. They must be uniform and equitable. They should be based, as far as practicable, on the taxpayer's ability to pay. They must serve a public purpose. They must not be unjust or confiscatory. And they must be collected by the local government itself, never by a private person.

Each source of revenue also has its own legal home. Real property tax comes from Title II of Book II of the Code, and the Special Education Fund levy from Section 235. Business taxes rest on Section 143, and the community tax on Sections 156 to 158. Regulatory fees and service charges, such as market stall rentals or slaughterhouse fees, come from the municipality's own revenue code, and regulatory fees in particular must stay in line with the actual cost of regulating.

This is also why the amount due is computed, not negotiated. It comes from the ordinance rate or the tax declaration, the same way for everyone. Adam Smith called this certainty: a good tax is one whose amount and timing are clear to the person paying it, not left to the mood of the collector.

What the Code Requires on the Spending Side

On the spending side, Section 305 starts with a flat ban: nothing leaves the local treasury without an appropriation ordinance or a law behind it. The same section goes on to say that public money is held in trust, may be spent only for public purposes, and must be properly documented and accounted for. I consider Section 305 the legal root of the whole ALTOS idea: in one section, the law draws the full circle that ALTOS is named for.

Section 344 then adds a series of checks before any payment, with each officer answering a different question:

Budget officer. Is there an appropriation for this purpose? In other words, did the Sanggunian authorize this kind of spending?

Accountant. Has the appropriation been obligated, and are the supporting documents complete? Is this a valid claim against it?

Treasurer. Is the cash actually there, in the right fund?

Local chief executive. Does the head of the local government approve the payment and accept responsibility for it?

Many large payments also follow a procurement. The New Government Procurement Act (RA 12009), signed in July 2024, replaced RA 9184. The treasurer does not run the bidding, but a contract that skipped the required procurement is a payment the treasurer should not make.

Why Spending Needs Extra Care

A mistake at the collection window and a mistake at the disbursing desk are not equal. Over-collecting or under-collecting is serious, but it usually involves money the government never had, and it can be corrected with the taxpayer. Money paid out without authority is different: it was already in the people's keeping, and once it leaves, recovering it is slow, costly and sometimes impossible. The Commission on Audit can disallow such a payment, and the officers who signed can be made to answer for it. That is why the law puts more locks on the door going out than on the door coming in.

A Simple Daily Test

This principle can be checked in seconds, at any counter, on any day:

Which ordinance or appropriation allows this?

If the answer is a specific section of the revenue code or a specific line in the approved budget, go ahead. If the answer is “we have always done it this way,” stop and look it up. Old habits are often right, but they are not a legal basis.

For the office as a whole, the question is a little bigger: can I name the law or ordinance behind every account that appears on our receipts? The proof that an office lives by this principle is simple to describe. The revenue code and the appropriation for every account are on file, and anyone who asks can be shown them.

Rules Change, So Keep Checking

Legality is not a box ticked once. Laws, circulars and manuals change often. The Local Treasury Operations Manual, the rules of the Commission on Audit, and the issuances of the Bureau of Local Government Finance (BLGF) are all revised from time to time. The Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RA 12001) of 2024, for example, requires a single Schedule of Market Values in each local government, prepared by the assessor and approved by the Department of Finance through the BLGF. Many local governments are now preparing revised schedules, which will change the very base the treasurer collects on. An office that is legal today can drift out of line next year without changing a thing. Before relying on any procedure, confirm that the text you are following is still the current one.

Where ALTOS Helps

In ALTOS, an official receipt cannot be issued for an item that is not linked to an income account in the office's chart of accounts, so every amount collected has a home in the books. The ALTOS Framework self-assessment goes further and lists fee items that have no revenue code reference, so gaps surface before an auditor finds them. The office then rates itself from 1 to 4 on each principle and starts with its two weakest areas.

The Foundation for the Other Nine

The next principles in the framework deal with forms, officers, deadlines and records. All of them assume the transaction was allowed in the first place. A perfectly filed receipt for a fee the law never created is still a wrong collection, just a well-documented one. So legality comes first, and everything else is built on top of it.

But legality has a weakness of its own: it cannot prove itself. Saying a payment was authorized is not the same as showing it. That is where the second principle comes in: every peso has a document.

Have you ever found a fee or a payment in your office with no clear legal basis? I'd love to hear how you handled it. Email me.

Why I Built ALTOS: Bringing Automation to Philippine Local Treasuries

A treasury system built around one idea: every peso should be accounted for from the moment it arrives to the moment it is reported.

Walk into many local treasury offices in the Philippines and you will still see stacks of receipts, hand-ruled cash books and monthly reports added up with a calculator. The people doing this work are careful and dedicated, but paper has limits. Reports take days to prepare, and a single wrong figure can hide for months before anyone notices.

I have spent more than 13 years in local government fiscal administration, and I kept asking the same question: what if the office's own rules were built into the tools it uses every day? That question became ALTOS, the Automated Local Treasury Operations System.

The Idea Behind It: Close the Circle

Picture the life of a single peso in a local treasury. It is received, recorded, deposited, perhaps paid out, and finally reported. At each of those stops, someone should be responsible for it. If even one stop has no clear owner, that is where errors and losses tend to happen.

Accountability has to go all the way around. A circle with a missing piece is not a circle, and public money slips out through the missing piece.

This is why I describe ALTOS as 360° accountability. Treasury work moves in a cycle of three steps: money comes in, money goes out, and both are reported. The reports then guide next year's targets and budget, and the cycle begins again.

Starting From Forms People Already Know

I did not want treasury staff to learn a strange new way of working. So every screen in ALTOS follows an official form they already fill out, from the LTOM and the COA. An auditor looking at the system sees the same documents they would see on paper.

The system also enforces the rules quietly in the background. Receipts are numbered strictly in sequence, so none can go missing. A check cannot carry a date earlier than its checkbook. The 20% Development Fund and other Trust Funds are always set aside. And because the RAAF and CRAAF are due on the 5th of each month, ALTOS shows a countdown so the officer and the supervisor both know how many days are left.

Two Subsystems, Both Ready

ALTOS is the main system, and it now has two working subsystems. The Treasury Collection System covers everything on the receiving side: official receipts, collectors and their receipt series, remittances, bank deposits, the daily report of collections, and the monthly accountability reports. The Treasury Disbursement System covers the paying side: vouchers, checks, cash advances and their liquidation, the check register, and disbursement reports. Both share one database, which can be used from a desktop application or a web browser anywhere on the office network.

A Record You Can Trust

A treasury's records are only as good as their protection against tampering. In ALTOS, each entry in the activity log is digitally linked to the one before it, much like links in a chain. If anyone deletes or alters an entry, the break in the chain shows. Mistakes can still be fixed, but only through a recorded correction that states who made it and why.

Security follows the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, an internationally used guide. Passwords are stored in scrambled form, accounts lock after repeated wrong attempts, idle sessions close on their own, and backups are encrypted and tested to make sure they can actually be restored.

Made to Last Beyond Its Builder

Treasurers are transferred, retire or move on. A good system should keep working after they leave. That is why ALTOS has a turnover feature that gathers and checks the office's records and prepares a certificate for the next treasurer.

Adoption Needs a Policy That Protects the Builder

ALTOS is not a demo or a school project. It runs on real collections and real disbursements, and the reports it produces are the ones an office signs and submits. When an office adopts a system like this, the system becomes part of how public money is handled, and that calls for clear rules on paper.

Without those rules, the builder carries risks that nobody else sees. The system can be copied or changed without the builder's knowledge. The builder can be expected to fix problems at any hour, for free, long after leaving the office. Credit for the work can quietly disappear. And if something goes wrong because of a change someone else made, the builder can still be the one blamed.

There is also a legal question. Under the Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293), there is no copyright in a work of the Government, meaning a work an official creates as part of regularly prescribed duties. Writing software is not among a treasurer's duties under the law, but the answer in each case depends on the facts and on what the parties agree in writing. That is exactly why the agreement has to come first.

What a Good Adoption Policy Covers

Proof of authorship. A dated record of the source files, design notes and versions that shows who built the system and when.

Registration. Where appropriate, registration or deposit of the work with the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL).

A written agreement. A memorandum of agreement or license that states what the office may and may not do with the system: how it may be used, who maintains and hosts it, who may change it, and what happens when the builder is transferred, retires or resigns.

Clear ownership of the data. The office's records belong to the office and must always be available to it and to auditors, while the software itself remains the builder's work.

Fair responsibility. The builder answers for the system as delivered, not for changes made by others or for how it is operated after turnover.

Legal review. Advice from legal counsel before signing, and before any commercial use.

A clear agreement is not a sign of distrust. It is how both sides keep their promises: the office keeps a working system and its records, the builder keeps the authorship, and taxpayers keep uninterrupted service.

I am also putting the thinking behind ALTOS into a book, 360° Accountability: Public Fiscal Administration in Philippine Local Treasuries. It closes with ten principles that any local treasury can follow, whether or not it uses software. I will write about each of them here.

Every peso, every step, every officer: 360°.

Views here are my own and do not represent any government office.
